analogy.p: Imagine each acid molecule as a person holding a balloon (the H+). A strong acid is a crowd where everyone lets go of their balloon the moment they enter the room, so the room is full of floating balloons (a high H+ concentration and a low pH). A weak acid is a crowd where only a few people let go, and most keep holding on, and sometimes people grab a balloon back, so the room has few free balloons (a lower H+ concentration and a higher pH). The analogy breaks down because in reality the balloons are charged ions and the process is a continual dynamic equilibrium rather than people making a choice.
analogy.t: Weak and strong acids as a crowd leaving a room

bullets: Functional group: **-COOH**, written in a displayed formula as C(=O)-O-H.
General formula: **CnH2n+1COOH**; each member differs by a **CH2** unit.
Names end in **-oic acid**: the stem shows the number of carbons (including the C in -COOH).
Contain only **C, H and O** and only **covalent bonds**.
They are **weak acids**, not strong acids like hydrochloric acid.
Prepared by **oxidation of alcohols**, linking to the alcohols topic.
The -COOH group is the part that reacts; the carbon chain is mostly unreactive.
core.p: **Carboxylic acids** are a **homologous series** of organic compounds whose molecules contain the **functional group -COOH** (the carboxyl group). In this group one carbon atom has a **double bond to an oxygen atom** and a **single bond to an -OH group**, so the carbon forms four bonds in total. Because every member carries the same functional group, all carboxylic acids have **similar chemical properties**, while their physical properties change gradually with chain length. They contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen joined by **covalent bonds**, so they are **simple molecular** compounds. The name ends in **-oic acid**, and you must be able to recognise one from its name or its formula.

bullets: **Methanoic acid: HCOOH** (one carbon; found in ant and nettle stings).
**Ethanoic acid: CH3COOH** (two carbons; main acid in **vinegar**).
**Propanoic acid: C2H5COOH** or CH3CH2COOH (three carbons).
**Butanoic acid: C3H7COOH** or CH3CH2CH2COOH (four carbons; smell of rancid butter).
Molecular formulae: methanoic CH2O2, ethanoic C2H4O2, propanoic C3H6O2, butanoic C4H8O2.
In the displayed formula the **O-H hydrogen** is the one that is released as H+ when the acid ionises.
Common mistake: counting the carbon in -COOH separately, e.g. calling CH3COOH 'propanoic acid'.
core.h: The first four members: names, formulae and displayed formulae
core.p: You must know the first four carboxylic acids: **methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid**, with 1, 2, 3 and 4 carbon atoms respectively. The number of carbons includes the carbon of the -COOH group, which is a frequent source of errors: ethanoic acid has **two** carbons, one in CH3 and one in COOH. In a displayed formula you must show **all** the bonds, including the **C=O double bond** and the **O-H bond**, and each carbon must have four bonds, each O two bonds and each H one bond.

bullets: Boiling points increase down the series: about **101, 118, 141, 164 °C**.
Reason: larger molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces**, so more energy is needed to separate them; covalent bonds are **not** broken.
Smaller members dissolve in water; solubility **decreases** with chain length.
Pure ethanoic acid freezes at about **17 °C**, so it can solidify in a cold lab (**glacial** ethanoic acid).
Smell: ethanoic acid has the sharp smell of **vinegar**, butanoic acid smells of rancid butter or vomit.
They do **not conduct** as pure liquids; in water the few ions formed allow weak conduction.
Link: same type of trend as for alkanes and alcohols.
core.p: Carboxylic acids are **simple molecular** substances, so they have **low melting and boiling points** compared with ionic compounds, and they do not conduct electricity because they have no free ions in the pure liquid. They have higher boiling points than alcohols and alkanes of similar size (methanoic about 101 °C, ethanoic about 118 °C, propanoic about 141 °C, butanoic about 164 °C). Within the series, boiling points **increase gradually** as the chain gets longer because the **intermolecular forces** between larger molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome. The first members dissolve easily in water, and solubility decreases as the chain length increases.

bullets: Solution is **acidic**, pH **below 7** (about 3 to 5 for dilute solutions).
Universal indicator: **orange/yellow**; litmus turns **red**; methyl orange **red**.
The H+ ions come from the **O-H** in the -COOH group.
Reversible ionisation: **CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO- + H+** (use the ⇌ sign).
Ethanoate ion is CH3COO-, methanoate HCOO-, propanoate C2H5COO-.
Contrast: ethanol in water is **neutral**, hydrochloric acid in water has **pH about 1**.
Link: all acids release H+ ions in water; the difference between strong and weak acids is **how far** they ionise.
core.h: Dissolving in water to form acidic solutions
core.p: Carboxylic acids **dissolve in water** to form **acidic solutions**. Some of the molecules **ionise**, releasing **hydrogen ions (H+)** from the -COOH group, and it is the H+ ions that make a solution acidic. Because the solution contains an excess of H+ over OH-, the pH is **below 7**: typically about **3 to 5** for solutions of the first members, and universal indicator turns **orange or yellow**. This is in contrast to alcohols, which form neutral solutions. The ionisation is shown as a **reversible reaction**: CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO- + H+.

bullets: **Weak acid** = acid that is **partially ionised** in aqueous solution (reversible, ⇌).
**Strong acid** = acid that is **completely ionised** (HCl → H+ + Cl-).
**Same concentration** (e.g. 0.1 mol/dm3): HCl has pH about **1**, ethanoic acid pH about **3**.
Definition of pH (Higher tier): pH = -log10[H+], so a strong monoprotic acid of concentration 0.01 mol/dm3 has pH **2**.
Do **not** confuse strong and weak with **concentrated** and **dilute**: concentration is how much acid is dissolved; strength is how far it ionises.
A weak acid still **neutralises the same amount of alkali** as the same moles of a strong acid, because the ionisation is reversible and continues as H+ is used up.
Weak acids react **more slowly** with metals and carbonates than strong acids of the same concentration because the H+ concentration is lower.
Exam wording: **"carboxylic acids do not ionise completely in water"**.
core.h: Weak acids and the effect on pH (Higher tier)
core.p: Carboxylic acids are **weak acids** because they **do not ionise completely** when dissolved in water. In a solution of ethanoic acid, **most** of the acid is present as unreacted **CH3COOH molecules** and only a small fraction has released H+ ions, so the solution has a **low concentration of H+** compared with a strong acid. This means an aqueous solution of a weak acid has a **higher pH** than a solution of a strong acid **with the same concentration**. Strong acids such as hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acid **ionise completely**. The pH scale is logarithmic, so a tenfold change in H+ concentration changes the pH by one unit.

bullets: General word equation: **carboxylic acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide**.
Example: ethanoic acid + sodium carbonate → sodium ethanoate + water + carbon dioxide.
Balanced: **2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2**.
With calcium carbonate: **2CH3COOH + CaCO3 → (CH3COO)2Ca + H2O + CO2**.
Observation: **fizzing**, solid carbonate **dissolves/disappears**.
Test for carbon dioxide: bubble through **limewater** → turns **cloudy/milky**.
Test to distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol: add sodium carbonate; **acid fizzes**, **alcohol does not**.
Descaling link: ethanoic acid (vinegar) dissolves limescale (calcium carbonate).
core.p: Carboxylic acids **react with carbonates** (and hydrogencarbonates) to produce a **salt, water and carbon dioxide**. This is the **same reaction** as any other acid with a carbonate and it is a standard test to show that a compound is an acid: you see **fizzing (effervescence)** and the gas turns **limewater cloudy**. The salt formed is named from the acid: ethanoic acid forms **ethanoates**, methanoic acid forms **methanoates**, propanoic acid forms **propanoates**. Alcohols do not react with carbonates, which makes this a good test to tell the two apart.

bullets: Word equation: **carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water**.
Example: **ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water**.
Symbol equation: **CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O**.
Conditions: **warm** (water bath), **few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid** as **catalyst**.
Naming: **alcohol part first (-yl) then acid part (-oate)**: methanol + propanoic acid → methyl propanoate.
Ester properties: **sweet, fruity smell**, low boiling point, **volatile**, insoluble or poorly soluble in water.
Uses: **artificial flavourings** and **perfumes**.
Safety: concentrated sulfuric acid is **corrosive**; alcohols are **flammable**, so use a **water bath** rather than a Bunsen.
core.p: Carboxylic acids **react with alcohols** in the presence of an **acid catalyst** (usually concentrated sulfuric acid) to produce **esters** and water. The reaction is called **esterification** and is **reversible**. Esters have the functional group **-COO-** and are known for their **sweet, fruity smells**, so they are used in **perfumes and food flavourings**. The name of an ester has two parts: the first word comes from the **alcohol** (ethanol gives **ethyl**) and the second from the **acid** (ethanoic acid gives **ethanoate**), so ethanoic acid and ethanol make **ethyl ethanoate**.

bullets: Acid + **metal** → salt + hydrogen: **Mg + 2CH3COOH → (CH3COO)2Mg + H2**.
Acid + **alkali** → salt + water: **CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2O**.
Acid + **metal oxide/hydroxide** → salt + water.
The salts of ethanoic acid are called **ethanoates**.
Reactions are **slower** than with a strong acid of the same concentration because [H+] is lower.
Higher tier: because the reaction removes H+, more acid ionises to replace it, so **the reaction goes to completion**.
Link to titration: ethanoic acid can be titrated with NaOH (use **phenolphthalein**).
core.p: Because carboxylic acids release H+ ions, they show the usual **acid reactions**, only more slowly than strong acids. They react with **reactive metals** such as magnesium to give a **salt and hydrogen**, and with **bases and alkalis** (neutralisation) to form a **salt and water**. For example, ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to form **sodium ethanoate** and water. You need to know the main specification reactions (water, carbonates, alcohols), but this wider pattern helps you answer unfamiliar questions by relating them to acids you have already studied.

bullets: Word equation: **ethanol + oxygen → ethanoic acid + water**.
Using [O]: **CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O**.
Microbial oxidation by **bacteria** (e.g. Acetobacter) in air gives **vinegar** from wine or cider.
Oxidising agent in the lab: **acidified potassium dichromate(VI)** (orange → green) (extra detail).
Methanol → methanoic acid, ethanol → ethanoic acid, propanol → propanoic acid, butanol → butanoic acid.
The reaction needs **oxygen**; this is why wine goes sour when exposed to **air**.
Pathway: ethene → ethanol (hydration) → ethanoic acid (oxidation) → ethyl ethanoate (esterification).
core.h: Making carboxylic acids: oxidation of alcohols
core.p: Carboxylic acids are made when **alcohols are oxidised**. This can happen by reaction with an **oxidising agent** (for example acidified potassium dichromate), or by **microbial action**: if a bottle of wine is left open, bacteria in the air **oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid**, and the wine turns into **vinegar**. In terms of the formula, the CH2OH at the end of the alcohol becomes COOH. This links the alcohol, carboxylic acid and ester topics into one sequence: **alkene → alcohol → carboxylic acid → ester**.

bullets: **Vinegar**: about **5 % ethanoic acid**; food flavouring and **preservative** (low pH prevents bacteria growing).
**Descaling**: reacts with **calcium carbonate** limescale to form soluble calcium ethanoate, water and CO2.
**Esters** made from acids: perfumes and food flavourings.
**Polyesters** are made from carboxylic acid monomers (condensation polymerisation).
**Soap**: made from the salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (fatty acids).
**Methanoic acid** is used in leather making and as a preservative/antibacterial agent in animal feed.
Link to next topics: carboxylic acids with two -COOH groups are monomers for condensation polymerisation.
core.p: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives have many everyday uses. **Ethanoic acid** is the acid in **vinegar** (about 5 % solution), which is used as a **food preservative**, **flavouring** and to **dissolve limescale** in kettles. Carboxylic acids are used to make **esters**, which are used as **perfumes and flavourings**, and some are used to make **polymers** and medicines (for example, aspirin is made from a related acid). The **sodium salts** of long-chain carboxylic acids are the basis of **soaps**. When you evaluate uses, you should link the property (acidic, reacts with carbonates, forms esters) to the use.

bullets: **Carboxylic acid vs alcohol**: add **sodium carbonate** → acid **fizzes** (CO2), alcohol **no reaction**; or add **universal indicator** → acid **orange/yellow**, alcohol **green**.
**Alkene vs alkane**: add **bromine water** → alkene turns **colourless**, alkane stays **orange**.
**Alcohol vs alkane**: alcohol **dissolves/mixes in water**, alkane does not; alcohol reacts with **sodium**.
Test for CO2: **limewater turns cloudy**.
pH: carboxylic acid **3 to 5**, alcohol **7**, strong acid **0 to 2**.
Remember all three: observation, **name the product** (e.g. carbon dioxide) and conclusion (e.g. 'it is a carboxylic acid').
Higher tier: use data (pH, fizzing rate) to decide between strong and weak acid.
core.h: Distinguishing tests and comparing with alcohols and alkenes
core.p: Examination questions frequently ask you to **identify or distinguish** compounds from their reactions. The key is to link a **functional group** to a **test**: the **-COOH** group gives an **acidic solution and fizzes with carbonate**; the **-OH** group of an alcohol gives a **neutral solution** and reacts with **sodium**; the **C=C** group of an alkene **decolourises bromine water**. Always state **both the test and the observation**, and then the conclusion, because a 2 or 3 mark question needs all three. Remember that carboxylic acids also react with sodium (as acids do), but sodium alone cannot distinguish an acid from an alcohol, so use a carbonate or an indicator.

bullets: **Moles = mass ÷ Mr**; Mr of CH3COOH = **60**.
Gas volume at room temperature and pressure = **moles × 24 dm3**.
Ratio in 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → …: **2 mol acid gives 1 mol CO2**.
Concentration = moles ÷ volume (dm3); 0.1 mol/dm3 means 0.1 mol in 1 dm3.
Rate questions: compare **rate of CO2 production** with strong and weak acid; the strong acid is **faster** at the start.
State **units** in all answers (g, dm3, mol/dm3).
Check your equation is **balanced** before you use the ratio.
core.h: Required skills: calculations and data with carboxylic acids
core.p: Although there is no required practical specific to carboxylic acids, you can be asked to apply **mole calculations**, **gas volume** and **pH** to the reactions above. For a calculation you should write the balanced equation, convert mass to moles using **moles = mass ÷ Mr**, use the **ratio** in the equation, and convert back to mass or volume (**1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3 at room temperature and pressure**). For pH data questions, remember that a **lower pH** means a higher H+ concentration and that a **weak acid** gives a **higher pH** than a strong acid at the same concentration.

exam: **1 mark recall**: functional group **-COOH**; names of first four acids (methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic); gas from acid + carbonate is **carbon dioxide**.
**Draw questions**: show every atom and every bond; the C=O double bond and O-H bond must both be drawn; check each carbon has four bonds.
**Equation questions (2 marks)**: correct formulae (1) and balancing (1): **2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2**; learn the pattern salt + water + carbon dioxide.

**'Explain why ethanoic acid is a weak acid' (2 marks)**: (1) it **does not ionise completely** / only partially ionised in water; (2) so fewer H+ ions are released / equilibrium lies on the side of molecules.
**pH comparison (Higher tier, 2 to 3 marks)**: weak acid has a **higher pH** than a strong acid of the **same concentration** because it has a **lower concentration of H+ ions**.
**Ester questions**: state reactants (carboxylic acid + alcohol), the **acid catalyst** and products (**ester + water**); name by alcohol first then acid, e.g. **ethyl ethanoate**.
**Describe a test (3 marks)**: add sodium carbonate (reagent); **fizzing/bubbles** (observation); gas turns **limewater cloudy** so it is CO2 and the compound is a carboxylic acid (conclusion).
**Calculations (3 to 4 marks)**: write the balanced equation, calculate moles, use ratio, convert to mass or volume; show each step and give units (g, dm3).

**Comparison questions (4 marks)**: compare alcohols and carboxylic acids using 'whereas': alcohol -OH, neutral in water, no reaction with carbonate; acid -COOH, acidic pH 3 to 5, fizzes with carbonate.

**6 mark extended response**: plan the route **ethene → ethanol → ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate**, give the reagent and conditions at each step, and name the type of reaction (addition/hydration, oxidation, esterification).
**Data questions**: when given pH values or rate data, quote numbers and say 'lower pH means more acidic', 'steeper graph means faster rate'.

mistakes.r: Weak/strong describes how far the acid ionises; dilute/concentrated describes the amount of acid in the solution.
mistakes.w: Saying a weak acid is a dilute acid (and a strong acid is concentrated).

mistakes.r: They are weak because they do not ionise completely in water (only partially ionised, reversible).
mistakes.w: Saying carboxylic acids are weak because they have a low concentration.

mistakes.r: Count all carbons including the -COOH carbon: CH3COOH has 2 carbons, so ethanoic acid.
mistakes.w: Calling CH3COOH 'propanoic acid' because it has a CH3 and a COOH.

mistakes.r: One O is double bonded to the carbon (C=O) and the other is -O-H: -C(=O)-O-H.
mistakes.w: Drawing the -COOH group as C-O-O-H or with two OH groups.

mistakes.r: Acid + carbonate gives carbon dioxide; test with limewater (turns cloudy). Hydrogen comes from acid + metal.
mistakes.w: Saying the gas from acid + carbonate is hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Both react with sodium. Use sodium carbonate (only the acid fizzes) or universal indicator.
mistakes.w: Saying alcohols and acids can be distinguished by adding sodium.

mistakes.r: The alcohol gives the first word (-yl) and the acid gives the second (-oate): ethyl ethanoate.
mistakes.w: Naming the ester from ethanoic acid + ethanol as 'ethanol ethanoate' or 'ethanoic ethyl'.

mistakes.r: Both are reversible reactions; use the ⇌ sign.
mistakes.w: Writing a single arrow for ionisation and esterification.

mistakes.r: The weak acid has the higher pH, because fewer H+ ions are present.
mistakes.w: Saying 'the pH of ethanoic acid is lower than HCl at the same concentration'.

summary: The specification asks you to know that carboxylic acids contain the functional group -COOH, to name and draw the first four members (methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid), and to describe their reactions: they dissolve in water to give acidic solutions, react with carbonates to produce carbon dioxide, and react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to produce esters. At Higher tier you must explain that they are weak acids because they do not ionise completely, so their solutions have a higher pH than strong acids of the same concentration. It matters because carboxylic acids link alcohols, esters and polymers in organic chemistry.

terms.d: A member of the homologous series containing the -COOH functional group, with general formula CnH2n+1COOH.
The atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic reactions of a compound; for carboxylic acids it is -COOH.
A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, similar chemical properties and gradually changing physical properties.
An acid that does not ionise completely when dissolved in water, so only some of its molecules release H+ ions.
An acid that ionises completely in water, such as hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acid.
To form ions; an acid ionises by releasing hydrogen ions when it dissolves in water.
A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants, shown with the sign ⇌.
A compound with the -COO- functional group, made when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol; often sweet-smelling.
The reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to form an ester and water.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is not used up.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen; alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids.
A scale from 0 to 14 that measures acidity or alkalinity; a solution with pH below 7 is acidic.
The ion that makes a solution acidic; its concentration determines the pH.
A compound containing the CO3 2- ion, which reacts with acids to produce carbon dioxide.
The amount of solute dissolved per unit volume of solution, e.g. mol/dm3; not the same as acid strength.
A dilute solution of ethanoic acid (about 5 %) used in cooking and as a preservative.

worked.q: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid reacts with excess sodium carbonate: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2. Calculate (a) the mass and (b) the volume at room temperature and pressure of carbon dioxide produced. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm3.) (5 marks)
steps: Ratio from equation: **2 mol acid : 1 mol CO2**, so moles CO2 = 0.10 ÷ 2 = **0.050 mol**.

worked.ans: pH of X = 2. Y has a higher pH because ethanoic acid is only partially ionised, so it has a lower concentration of H+ ions than HCl of the same concentration.
worked.q: Solution X is 0.010 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. Solution Y is 0.010 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid. Calculate the pH of X and explain why the pH of Y is higher. (Higher tier, 4 marks)
steps: HCl is a **strong acid**, so it ionises completely: [H+] = **0.010 mol/dm3**.
Ethanoic acid is a **weak acid**: it does **not ionise completely**, so most of it stays as CH3COOH molecules.
So [H+] in Y is **lower** than 0.010 mol/dm3, so the pH is **higher than 2** (about 3 to 4).

worked.ans: Model answer: Mix ethanoic acid with ethanol, add a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst and warm in a hot water bath. Ethyl ethanoate and water form (the reaction is reversible) and the ester is recognised by its sweet, fruity smell. Esters are used in perfumes and food flavourings.
worked.q: Describe how you would make a sample of ethyl ethanoate and state one use of esters. (4 marks)
steps: Mix **ethanoic acid** and **ethanol** in a test tube/flask.
Add a few drops of **concentrated sulfuric acid** as a **catalyst**.
**Warm** the mixture in a **hot water bath** (not a naked flame because ethanol is flammable).
Products are **ethyl ethanoate and water**; detect the ester by its **sweet, fruity smell**; use: **perfumes or food flavourings**.
